title: SKU Rationalization: The True Cost of SKU Expansion
summary: New flavors can add complexity faster than profit. Learn how SKU rationalization helps beverage leaders focus on products that pay off.
body_markdown:
Walk into any[beverage company](https://www.cbiz.com/industries/food-beverage) strategy meeting, and you’ll hear the same conversation: consumers want innovation. Retailers want newness. Competitors are launching new flavors and package formats. The pressure to expand the product portfolio is constant.


In many cases, the race to serve all masters results in SKU expansion that creates complexity much faster than it creates profit. That’s where SKU rationalization comes in.


## Every New SKU Has a Hidden Cost


Adding a new flavor might seem like a low-risk growth opportunity. In reality, every new SKU introduces additional inventory, forecasting challenges, packaging components, production scheduling requirements, regulatory considerations, distributor inventory, and sales support. What looks like one new product on a shelf can create dozens of new decisions for your operations, finance, and sales teams behind the scenes.


And the impact goes beyond logistics. There are very real financial consequences, too.


## Where Your Profit Goes


Many companies evaluate a potential SKU by estimating expected sales volume and gross revenue. Far fewer evaluate the full cost of supporting that SKU throughout the supply chain. New products frequently require smaller production runs, which increase per-unit costs. They can create additional changeovers and downtime on production lines. They often require unique packaging materials that lose the purchasing leverage associated with larger orders. The result is a phenomenon that finance leaders encounter regularly: revenue grows while profitability stagnates.


## SKU Profitability: Not All Volume Is Profitable Volume


The most successful beverage brands understand that not all volume is profitable volume. They analyze SKU profitability, evaluating both gross margin percentage and gross margin dollars. They examine inventory turns, production complexity, and channel performance. Most importantly, they understand the strategic role each product plays within the portfolio. A seasonal release that reinforces brand identity may deserve its place despite modest financial returns. A low-margin line extension with minimal incremental sales likely doesn’t.


The challenge is that product decisions are often emotional. Founders may feel attached to a product. Sales teams may point to retailer requests. Marketing teams may highlight consumer interest. Without disciplined financial analysis, the organization can confuse activity with value creation.


## Three SKU Rationalization Questions Before You Add the Next Flavor


Growth-stage beverage companies should regularly ask three questions:


- Is this SKU generating attractive margins?
- Is it creating operational complexity?
- Would the business be better if that production capacity were allocated elsewhere?


SKU rationalization isn’t about eliminating innovation. It’s about ensuring innovation creates value.


In today’s market, focus is frequently a greater competitive advantage than variety. The brands that win aren’t necessarily those with the most products. They’re the brands that understand exactly which products deserve their attention, resources, and capital.


If you’re weighing which products deserve a spot in your lineup, our food and beverage professionals can help you evaluate SKU-level profitability and focus on the products that move your business forward.Reach out to start the conversation .


#### Frequently Asked Questions


Look beyond sales totals. Compare each product’s margin, in both percentage and dollars, against the extra production time, packaging, inventory, and support it requires. A strong seller can still drain profit once you count those costs.


Each addition tends to shrink production runs, add downtime between batches, and spread packaging purchases across more materials. Costs climb with every one of those shifts, so revenue can rise while profit stays flat.


Strategic value counts, too. A product that reinforces your brand, such as a seasonal release, can justify a smaller margin. One that adds complexity without bringing in meaningful new sales is a stronger candidate to retire.
